Listen to this article Share Weekly Summary: Nigeria and Africa’s development challenges are increasingly defined not by a shortage of resources, opportunities or policy ideas, but by the failure to convert them into tangible improvements in people’s lives. This week’s contributions examine that problem from different perspectives, ranging from the politics of economic relief and Africa’s gold-refining ambitions to climate preparedness, ethnic relations, reparative justice, corruption and institutional accountability. Together, they raise a fundamental question: what does it take to turn national potential and public commitments into outcomes that citizens can see, experience and trust? The discussion begins with the gap between economic stabilisation and household welfare. Vincent Nwanma questions whether the Federal Government’s 90-day cost-of-living intervention will provide meaningful relief or become entangled in the politics of the approaching elections. Faith Omoboye extends the conversation to Africa’s mineral wealth, arguing that the continent must move beyond exporting raw gold and build the refining capacity, technical expertise and supporting industries needed to retain more value locally. Sunday Ene-Ojo Atawodi brings the discussion to climate security, insisting that Nigeria must translate El Niño warnings into early assistance, agricultural protection, water management and practical preparedness for vulnerable communities. Richard Ikiebe examines another dimension of national development: the burden of ethnic prejudice and the Igbo community’s struggle to reconcile individual enterprise with collective political organisation. Bunmi Oyinsan, meanwhile, interrogates Africa’s debt burden through the question of historical responsibility, proposing that reparative justice should contribute to more equitable development financing rather than remain confined to symbolic apologies. The final contributions confront the institutional weaknesses that threaten to undermine these ambitions. Francis Egbokhare describes Nigeria’s growing scam economy as a system in which bribery, rent-seeking, institutional capture and deception increasingly compete with productive enterprise. His argument raises serious questions about the integrity of institutions responsible for managing public resources. Joachim Adenusi offers a practical response through a unified promise-tracking framework that would enable governments and businesses to measure commitments, monitor implementation and identify failures before deadlines are missed. Taken together, the articles suggest that development requires more than political will or financial resources. It demands institutions that can translate intentions into results, protect public interest and hold those entrusted with responsibility accountable. The common thread: A recurring concern across this week’s contributions is the difference between possessing an advantage and making it work for the public good. Nigeria may report improving macroeconomic indicators, but households struggling to afford food will judge recovery by their purchasing power. Africa may establish more gold refineries, but their contribution to development will depend on the jobs, industries, revenues and technological capabilities they create. Similarly, Nigeria may receive early warnings about climate risks, but those warnings have limited value unless governments act before communities lose their homes, crops and livelihoods. The distinction between potential and performance is therefore central to understanding the continent’s development difficulties. The articles also draw attention to the institutional and social conditions that determine whether resources and opportunities produce equitable outcomes. Ethnic prejudice, weak political cooperation, historical injustice, expensive borrowing and institutional corruption all influence how societies distribute opportunities and bear the costs of development. Ikiebe’s examination of Igbo identity reminds Nigerians that national cohesion requires fairness and a willingness to confront internal weaknesses without perpetuating collective stereotypes. Oyinsan’s discussion of reparations challenges the international financial system to recognise historical economic injustices while insisting that African governments must also address contemporary mismanagement. Egbokhare’s critique of the scam economy exposes how corruption and the commercialisation of public institutions undermine merit, trust and productive investment. These arguments reinforce the importance of institutions that protect fairness, encourage enterprise and make public resources serve collective interests. Ultimately, the week’s contributions point towards a more demanding standard of leadership and governance: measurable delivery. Economic relief must be reflected in household welfare; mineral processing must create domestic value; climate warnings must trigger timely protection; national unity must be built on equal citizenship; and reparative justice must contribute to sustainable productive capacity. Above all, public and private institutions must demonstrate that their commitments are being fulfilled. Adenusi’s proposed promise register provides a useful framework for this accountability, but its effectiveness will depend on independent verification, transparent reporting and consequences for persistent failure. Nigeria and Africa cannot afford to keep measuring progress by announcements, intentions or resources mobilised. The more important measure is what changes occur in the lives of citizens. Article Reviews: Monday, November 9; Ninety days to paradise? Nigeria’s cost-of-living crisis and the politics of economic relief – By Dr Vincent Nwanma Nwanma examines the Federal Government’s proposed 90-day programme to address the cost-of-living crisis, questioning whether it will deliver genuine household relief or become part of the political effort to shape public perceptions ahead of the 2027 elections. His distinction between declining inflation and actual improvements in living standards is particularly important, as households continue to struggle with food affordability and weakened purchasing power. He challenges the government to provide specific funding commitments, implementation responsibilities and measurable targets, while also demanding that opposition parties present credible alternatives rather than rely exclusively on political criticism. https://businessday.ng/pro/article/ninety-days-to-paradise-nigerias-cost-of-living-crisis-and-the-politics-of-economic-relief/ Article 2: Africa’s gold refining drive and the economics of capturing mineral wealth – By Faith Omoboye Omoboye examines Africa’s growing investment in domestic gold-refining capacity against the continent’s longstanding dependence on exporting raw minerals and importing higher-value products. She argues that refining can create employment, strengthen technical expertise and stimulate supporting industries but cautions that installed capacity alone does not guarantee commercial success. Her emphasis on international accreditation, responsible sourcing, formalising artisanal mining and developing local jewellery and manufacturing industries offers a practical framework for ensuring that Africa retains more of the economic value generated by its mineral resources. https://businessday.ng/pro/article/africas-gold-refining-drive-and-the-economics-of-capturing-mineral-wealth/ Tuesday, November 10; El Niño: Climate warnings and Nigeria’s preparedness for a potential climate risk – By Prof Sunday Ene-Ojo Atawodi Atawodi shifts attention from climate forecasting to the more urgent question of preparedness. Using the growing probability of a strong El Niño event, he argues that Nigeria must translate meteorological and hydrological information into practical interventions that protect farmers, households and vulnerable communities. His proposals include forecast-based cash transfers, timely distribution of agricultural inputs, improved water management, coordinated reservoir monitoring and clearly funded emergency responses. The article’s strongest argument is that early warnings should be judged by whether they enable people to protect their livelihoods before disaster strikes, not simply by whether government agencies issue alerts. https://businessday.ng/pro/article/el-nino-climate-warnings-and-nigerias-preparedness-for-a-potential-climate-risk/ Wednesday, November 11; The Igbo: Self-Defeat and the Burden of Being Misunderstood – By Dr Richard Ikiebe Ikiebe explores the historical prejudices and internal political contradictions that have shaped perceptions of the Igbo in Nigeria. He challenges colonial interpretations of Igbo political organisation, particularly the assumption that decentralised systems of authority represent an absence of governance, while also examining how individual independence and competing ambitions have complicated collective political action. Drawing on the Aba Women’s War and the enduring consequences of the Civil War, he makes a case for national reintegration based on equal citizenship and fair treatment. His argument also challenges the Igbo to translate their considerable entrepreneurial strengths into greater political cooperation without surrendering their traditions of individual initiative. https://businessday.ng/pro/article/the-igbo-self-defeat-and-the-burden-of-being-misread/ Article 2; Africa’s debt: What we owe and what we are owed – By Dr Bunmi Oyinsan Oyinsan places Africa’s mounting debt obligations alongside the continent’s historical claims for reparative justice, questioning why contemporary financial liabilities are treated as enforceable obligations while the economic consequences of slavery and colonial extraction receive less practical recognition. She proposes that reparations could support development through grants, debt buybacks, financing guarantees and investment in productive capacity. Importantly, she does not present historical injustice as an excuse for contemporary mismanagement. Her argument insists on two responsibilities operating together: international recognition of historical obligations and stronger African institutions capable of preventing renewed cycles of unsustainable borrowing. https://businessday.ng/pro/article/africas-debt-what-we-owe-and-what-we-are-owed/ Thursday, November 12; Dirty money and the scam economy undermining Nigeria’s development – By Prof Francis Egbokhare Egbokhare presents a troubling account of how corruption, fraud, bribery and rent-seeking have become embedded in different aspects of Nigeria’s economic and institutional life. Moving beyond conventional discussions of public-sector corruption, he examines how the commercialisation of appointments, recruitment, contracts, training programmes, financial services and even philanthropy undermines merit and public trust. His description of Nigeria as a potential cartelised scam economy highlights the danger of a system in which access and deception offer more reliable routes to wealth than productive enterprise. He calls for sanctions that reach powerful insiders, transparent procurement and budget information, and a wider cultural rejection of everyday fraud and unexplained wealth. https://businessday.ng/pro/article/dirty-money-and-the-scam-economy-undermining-nigerias-development/ Friday, November 13; Tracking performance commitments to investors and citizens in Nigeria – By Dr Joachim Adenusi (Ogarisk) Adenusi proposes a practical framework for improving accountability by combining corporate performance-reporting methods with existing government delivery mechanisms. He argues that every major commitment should have a responsible officer, baseline, measurable target, deadline, funding source and independent means of verification. Drawing lessons from corporate key performance indicators, federal performance bonds and the World Bank-supported SFTAS programme, he recommends a public promise register incorporating early-warning indicators to identify implementation problems before deadlines are missed. His proposal to pilot the framework with a willing state and a listed company or public-private infrastructure project offers a realistic starting point for extending transparent performance monitoring to all 774 local government councils. https://businessday.ng/pro/article/tracking-performance-commitments-to-investors-and-citizens-in-nigeria/ Closing Reflection: The central message of this week’s contributions is that development cannot be sustained on promises, political narratives or the possession of resources alone. It depends on the institutions, values and practical decisions that determine how those resources are managed and how opportunities are distributed. Nigeria and Africa need leaders who can demonstrate results, institutions that protect public interest and citizens prepared to demand evidence of performance. Ultimately, the test of leadership is not what governments promise, but what people can point to as evidence that those promises have been fulfilled.
